The whole blockchain is available, but not open until an encryption puzzle is solved.

Once that puzzle is solved, it gets acknowledged as the current status quo of all bitcoin transactions, including these latest changes.

If someone was able to link your key to your identity, yes, they would have your complete transaction history. You can generate new keys anytime from your wallet though, so then that key is only valid from transactions as of that time.

Never reusing an address does significantly improve your privacy, however there are some tools currently available that can dramatically improve it, even so far as to make your finances entirely anonymous if you wish.

The CoinJoin algorithm mixes your transaction with many other peoples transactions in such a way that you don't have to trust anyone (all done with cool math tricks,) and makes it very difficult to identify who sent what where - even if you knew who was who. The Send Shared feature the blockchain.info wallet offers will repeat this CoinJoin transaction multiple times which significantly reduces the confidence of any analysis. As in - "there's a 1% chance these coins originated from there."

Simply sending coin to a pooled wallet and then withdrawing them also breaks the connection to your identity - providing you trust the operator of the pooled wallet. Example - an exchange like BTC-e, or an anonymous mixing service.

There is a new maths technology called Zero-Knowledge proofs that will provide absolute and total anonymity. It's not yet available. The Zerocoin project is real, but I think they're waiting for the digital economy to develop some more before they release. Besides, releasing Zerocoin as an altcoin isn't the best way to go about it. Once Bitcoin has double-pegged sidechains enabled zerocoin could be implemented as a sidechain. We'll just have to wait and find out, I suppose.

This transparency is an advantage if you're running a public entity - like a corporation - and need to be able to prove that you haven't embezzled a dime.
